To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the interaction between the antitumor drug chartreusin and DNA is enthalpy driven and that the binding enthalpies and the heat capacities of binding can be determined by ITC and DSC.
the interaction of chartreusine with DNA is enthalpy driven and the hydrophobic transfer from water to the DNA intercalfing site is the main contribution to the binding free energy.
chartreusin binds to DNA by intercalation and minor groove interactions and the thermodynamics of the interaction are enthalpy driven.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the thermodynamics of the interaction between DNA and the antitumor drug chartreusin.
the development of a thermodynamic database of the interactions of small molecules with DNA and with the application of the thermodynamic data to the design of drugs that bind to nucleic acids.
the development of a thermodynamic profile for a drug-DNA interaction, with a view to understanding how the different thermodynamic parameters contribute to the binding free energy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
chartreusin binds to DNA by a combination of intercalation and minor groove interactions.
the interaction of the chartreusion chromophore with the DNA is the main driving force in the DNA-drug binding process.
the binding of chartreusion to DNA is enthalpy driven and the binding is mainly driven by the hydrophobic transfer from the solution to intercalating site.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the thermodynamic parameters obtained for the chartreusins are very similar to those reported for the interaction of other intercalative drugs with DNA.
the thermodynamic characterization of drug-DNA interactions is a useful tool in rational drug design, especially in the case of multivalent drugs.
the binding of chartreuse to DNA is a very favorable process, driven by a favorable enthalpy, with an unfavorable entropy contribution.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the binding-induced heat capacity change is a key thermodynamic parameter for the characterization of DNA-drug interactions.
the thermodynamic profile for chartreusin binding is very similar to that for the binding of the intercalating dye ethidium.
a combination of ITC, UV melting and DSC experiments can provide a detailed thermodynamic description of the binding of a multivalent drug to DNA.
